questions.q: State the formula for the magnetic field at a point on the axial line of a short bar magnet of magnetic moment \(m\) at a distance \(r\) from its centre. Give the SI unit of each quantity.
questions.a: \(B_{\text{axial}} = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi} \frac{2m}{r^3}\). \(\mu_0/4\pi = 10^{-7} \, \text{T·m/A}\), \(m\) in A·m², \(r\) in m, \(B\) in T. A wrong answer (e.g., missing factor 2, using \(r^2\), or confusing axial/equatorial) reveals the student has not internalised the dipole analogy or the solenoid derivation.

questions.q: A bar magnet’s magnetic moment \(\vec{m}\) points north. At a point on the equatorial line, what is the direction of the magnetic field \(\vec{B}\) relative to \(\vec{m}\)? Explain using the electrostatic analogy.
questions.a: On the equatorial line, \(\vec{B}\) is anti-parallel to \(\vec{m}\) (points opposite to the magnetic moment). The electric dipole’s equatorial field is \(\vec{E}_{\text{eq}} = -\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{\vec{p}}{r^3}\); replacing \(\vec{E} \to \vec{B}\), \(\vec{p} \to \vec{m}\), \(1/4\pi\varepsilon_0 \to \mu_0/4\pi\) gives \(\vec{B}_{\text{eq}} = -\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi} \frac{\vec{m}}{r^3}\). A student who says “same direction” is confusing axial and equatorial fields or misapplying the analogy.

questions.q: A short bar magnet has magnetic moment \(0.48 \, \text{J/T}\). Calculate the magnitude of the magnetic field at a distance of \(10 \, \text{cm}\) from the centre on (a) the axial line, (b) the equatorial line. Use \(\mu_0/4\pi = 10^{-7} \, \text{T·m/A}\).
questions.a:
Given: \(m = 0.48 \, \text{A·m}^2\), \(r = 0.10 \, \text{m}\).  
(a) Axial: \(B = 10^{-7} \times \frac{2 \times 0.48}{(0.10)^3} = 10^{-7} \times \frac{0.96}{0.001} = 10^{-7} \times 960 = 9.6 \times 10^{-5} \, \text{T}\).  
(b) Equatorial: \(B = 10^{-7} \times \frac{0.48}{(0.10)^3} = 10^{-7} \times 480 = 4.8 \times 10^{-5} \, \text{T}\).  
A wrong answer often comes from using \(r\) in cm without converting to m (giving \(10^{-11}\) T), or forgetting the factor 2 in axial field.

questions.q: Two identical short bar magnets of moment \(m\) are placed coaxially with their north poles facing each other, separated by a distance \(2d\). Find the point on the line joining them where the net magnetic field is zero.
questions.a:
Let the point be at distance \(x\) from the centre of the left magnet (so \(x\) from left, \(2d - x\) from right). Both magnets produce axial fields pointing away from their north poles. For zero net field, magnitudes must be equal:  
\(\frac{2m}{x^3} = \frac{2m}{(2d - x)^3} \Rightarrow x = 2d - x \Rightarrow x = d\).  
The midpoint is the null point. A student who sets up the equation but forgets the \(r^3\) dependence (using \(r^2\)) will get a different answer, revealing confusion with Coulomb’s law.

questions.q: A student writes: “The magnetic field on the axis of a bar magnet is twice the field on the equator at the same distance.” Is this statement always correct? Justify.
questions.a: The statement is correct **only in magnitude** for a short dipole at the same distance \(r\): \(|B_{\text{axial}}| = 2|B_{\text{eq}}|\). However, the directions are different: axial field is parallel to \(\vec{m}\), equatorial is anti-parallel. If the student ignores direction or assumes the formula holds for \(r \sim l\), the statement is misleading. A complete answer must mention both magnitude ratio and directional difference, and the condition \(r \gg l\).

questions.q: Design a simple experiment using a compass needle and a bar magnet to verify that the magnetic field on the axial line is twice that on the equatorial line at the same distance. Outline the procedure and the measurements needed.
questions.a: Place the bar magnet on a sheet of paper with its axis along the east-west direction (to avoid Earth’s field interference). Mark the centre. At a fixed distance \(r\) (e.g., 10 cm) on the axial line, place a compass and note the deflection \(\theta_{\text{axial}}\) from east-west. Repeat on the equatorial line at the same \(r\) to get \(\theta_{\text{eq}}\). In a uniform field \(B\), \(\tan\theta \propto B\). Compute \(\tan\theta_{\text{axial}} / \tan\theta_{\text{eq}}\); it should be close to 2. A poor answer omits the need to eliminate Earth’s field or uses a single compass without a reference direction.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Observe iron ______ on a sheet of paper placed over a bar magnet (a common Class 12 lab activity).
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: Student can (1) calculate the magnitude and direction of the magnetic field at any axial or equatorial point of a bar magnet using the dipole formulas, (2) apply the electrostatic analogy to write the field expressions without memorising them separately, and (3) solve numerical problems involving superposition of fields from two magnets.
